steps.domain_action: Initialize the complex plane as the void state before defining the zeta function.
Apply analytic continuation to extend the zeta function into the critical strip.
Split the domain of nontrivial zeros into two branches: fixed on the critical line or moved off it.
Evaluate the T-arm where the zero is fixed on the critical line Re(s)=1/2.
Assert the identity of the zero as its own reflection in the T-arm.
Record the fixed zero as a permanent verified state on the critical line.
Evaluate the F-arm where the zero is moved off the critical line to a distinct partner.
Apply the reflection map s ↔ 1-s to the moved zero in the F-arm.
Compose the moved zero with its reflection to form a distinct pair.
Hold the paradoxical state where the zero is both fixed and moved simultaneously.
Rejoin the T-arm and F-arm to resolve the symmetry of the zero.
Anchor the resolved state within the global constraint of the functional equation.
Close the loop by asserting the self-reference of the entire system.

grounding_reasoning:
⊣=𐑥: The reflection symmetry exchanging $s$ and $1-s$ creates a cyclic closure where zeros either map to themselves or form closed pairs, mirroring the figure-8 or double-well topology of the functional equation's domain.
⊢=𐑦: The Riemann Hypothesis posits that all nontrivial zeros lie on the critical line, effectively collapsing the two-dimensional search space of the complex plane onto a one-dimensional boundary where the surface (the line) contains the full information of the bulk (the zeros).
⊞=𐑙: The hypothesis that every zero is its own reflection implies a perfect one-to-one symmetric pairing where no distinct partners exist off the critical line.
◻=𐑴: The reflection symmetry exchanging $s$ and $1-s$ constitutes a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry that protects the zeros on the critical line, requiring a symmetry-breaking perturbation to move them off the line.
⊙=⊙: The Riemann Hypothesis posits that all nontrivial zeros lie exactly on the critical line, representing a state where the system is precisely at the threshold of criticality with maximal symmetry and scale-free properties.
⊥=𐑓: The Riemann Hypothesis posits that all nontrivial zeros lie on the critical line, meaning they are fixed points of the reflection symmetry and thus achiral with no persistent symmetry breaking.
≻=𐑽: The reflection symmetry acts as a catalytic constraint that stabilizes the transition between conjugate states without being consumed, ensuring zeros remain on the critical line.
≺=𐑹: The hypothesis that every zero is its own reflection under the s ↔ 1-s transformation implies an exact Z2 symmetry at the critical line, corresponding to the provably exact Frobenius condition.
⋈=𐑐: The hypothesis that every zero is fixed on the critical line implies a rigid, geometry-enforcing constraint where the reflection symmetry holds with near-certainty, eliminating the probabilistic "moved" case.
⊤=𐑧: The hypothesis that all zeros lie on the critical line implies a state where the system is kinetically frozen into a symmetric configuration, resisting any rearrangement off the line without external driving.
∈=𐑔: The Riemann Hypothesis posits a global constraint where the symmetry of every zero across the entire critical strip is determined by the system's fundamental structure, implying scale-free propagation.
∋=𐑝: The reflection symmetry requires a zero to be paired with its specific counterpart (s and 1-s) simultaneously to satisfy the functional equation's constraint.
